issues.legal_issue: A government auction of public property conducted through collusion, material procedural irregularities, and disregard of the public authority’s duty to obtain a fair market price cannot stand.
material_facts: The disputed plots belonged to a public industrial development corporation, but it was not notified of their attachment or sale.
A bank’s claim that it held a mortgage over one plot was disregarded.
The sale proclamations did not adequately describe the property rights being sold, and the auction was not widely advertised.
The reserve prices were omitted from the sale records, although reserve prices had been fixed; bids far below those prices were accepted.
A court’s stay of recovery proceedings concerning one plot was ignored when the sale was confirmed.

The auction records falsely stated that the required initial deposits had been made immediately after the auction; the deposits were made the following day, and the remaining purchase price for one plot was never paid.
The evidence supported the conclusion that the purported auctions were collusive and that the public land was being acquired through manipulation of the process.
issues.conclusion: The auction sales were illegal, fraudulent, collusive, and mala fide, and the appeal challenging their setting aside was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The disposal of public property is in the nature of a trust, requiring public authorities to make all reasonable efforts to obtain the best available market price through a fair and transparent process. A government authority may not dispose of public property below the reserve price. The Court relied on Ram and Shyam Co. v. State of Haryana, (1985) 3 SCC 267; V. Purushotham Rao v. Union of India, (2001) 10 SCC 305; Aggarwal and Modi Enterprises (P.) Ltd. v. New Delhi Municipal Council, (2007) 8 SCC 75; Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies, (2009) 6 SCC 171; and Anil Kumar Srivastava v. State of U.P., (2004) 8 SCC 671. The recovery and sale process was governed by sections 279, 284, 286 and 341 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rules 273, 273-A, 282 and 285-A to 285-N of the 1952 Rules.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_public_property_auction and public_property_sold_for_recovery and owner_not_notified and (secured_claim_ignored or judicial_stay_ignored) and no_wide_auction_publicity and accepted_bid_below_reserve and (auction_record_misstated_deposit or purchase_balance_unpaid)

predicates.appeal_challenging_public_property_aucti: A party appealed a decision setting aside an auction of public property.
predicates.public_property_sold_for_recovery: A public asset was put up for auction to recover money owed to the government.
predicates.owner_not_notified: The authority conducting the sale did not notify the public body that owned the property about the attachment or sale.
predicates.secured_claim_ignored: The sale authority proceeded despite a creditor’s claim that it held security over the property.
predicates.judicial_stay_ignored: The sale authority proceeded with or confirmed a sale despite being informed of a court order staying the recovery proceedings.
predicates.no_wide_auction_publicity: The proposed auction was not publicized through means likely to give the public wide notice.
predicates.accepted_bid_below_reserve: The sale authority accepted a bid below a reserve price fixed for the property.
predicates.auction_record_misstated_deposit: The auction record stated that the required initial deposit was made immediately after the auction when it was actually made later.
predicates.purchase_balance_unpaid: The purchaser did not pay the full purchase price for the property.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a public-property recovery auction and the stated combination of failures and irregularities occurred, the auction is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A successful bidder at a recovery auction must make the required initial deposit immediately after the auction and pay the balance within the prescribed time.
material_facts: The auction conditions required the highest bidder to deposit one fourth of the bid immediately after the auction and the remainder within fifteen days.
The auction records stated that the initial deposits had been made immediately after the auctions, but the government register showed that they were made the next day.
The register showed that the remaining three fourths of the bid for one plot was never deposited, although a sale certificate was issued.
issues.conclusion: The required initial deposits were not made immediately after the auctions, and the full purchase price for one plot was not paid; the auction payment requirements were therefore breached.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 285-D of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952 requires the declared purchaser to deposit twenty-five per cent of the bid immediately, failing which the land must be put up for sale again. Rule 285-E requires payment of the full purchase price by the fifteenth day after the sale and provides for forfeiture and resale in case of default.

predicates.recovery_auction_payment_challenge: The dispute concerns payment obligations in an auction conducted to recover public dues.
predicates.initial_deposit_made_later_than_immediat: The successful bidder did not pay the required initial portion of the bid immediately after the auction.
predicates.purchase_balance_not_paid_within_require: The purchaser did not pay the remaining purchase price within the required time.

issues.definition: In a recovery-auction payment dispute, a delayed initial deposit or an unpaid balance means the auction payment requirements were breached.

issues.legal_issue: Exemplary costs may be imposed on appellants whose litigation seeks to sustain a fraudulent attempt to acquire public land.
material_facts: The appellants pursued an appeal concerning auction sales that the Court found fraudulent and collusive.
The Court found that the purported auctions were part of an attempt, involving the appellants and government officials, to grab public land.
issues.conclusion: The Court imposed exemplary costs on the appellants, payable to the Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee, with recovery as a fine under the Code of Criminal Procedure if proof of payment was not filed as directed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the litigation as requiring exemplary costs because the auction involved manipulation and an attempt to grab public land, and stated that litigation should not operate like a lottery offering an illegitimate windfall at only the cost of litigation. If proof of payment was not filed within the directed time, the costs were recoverable as a fine under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

predicates.appeal_concerning_public_land_auction: The appellants pursued an appeal concerning an auction of public land.
predicates.court_found_attempt_to_grab_public_land_: The Court found that the appellants and officials used manipulation in an attempt to acquire public land through the auction.

issues.definition: When appellants pursue an appeal concerning a public-land auction that the Court finds was manipulated in an attempt to acquire public land, exemplary costs are imposed on them.
